classification_signals: Abstract: 'This paper argues that the sublime is worth returning to as a designerly concept for landscape architecture due to its ability to reveal our interconnectedness to the world. The sublime is reconceptualized here as being a physiological event...'
Introduction (p. 2): 'This paper argues that the concept of the sublime is central to landscape architectural design practice and worth revisiting in a contemporary context.'

Introduction (p. 2): 'The following argument for understanding the sublime through a physiological mode builds on the work of Edmund Burke by entwining it with the contemporary neuroaesthetics of Antonio Damasio (1999).'

Section 'Primacy of Sensation' (p. 14): 'This section argues that experiencing the sublime can be understood as an event that involves concrete material relations between one's being and the environment it occupies.'

Section 'One Hand in the Dirt, One Hand on the Pen' (p. 20): 'Revisiting the writings of Thomas Whately, Uvedale Price, and Frederick Law Olmsted will illustrate how they experimented with the sublime or landscape aesthetics from a physiological basis.'
The paper does not present new empirical data, but rather synthesizes existing theories and historical design interpretations to propose a new conceptual framework.
title: Sensation and the Sublime: Revisiting the Physiological Basis of Aesthetic Encounter

findings.antecedent: Encounter with landscape (spatio-temporal relation between one's body and its environment)
findings.consequent: Disruption of predetermined or habitual responses; physiological event (the sublime)
findings.quote: The sublime is reconceptualized here as being a physiological event that occurs between one's body and the landscape, as opposed to the commonly held psychological or subjective understanding.

findings.antecedent: Encounter with landscape (suggestion of danger, critical distance from source)
findings.consequent: Bodily reactions associated with fear; physiological changes (Burke's sublime)
findings.quote: According to Burke, the sublime in an encounter with landscape emerged from the mind's suggestion of danger, prompting bodily reactions associated with fear.

findings.antecedent: Objects of infinite scale (mathematical sublime, Kant)
findings.consequent: Imagination challenged; reason intervenes by expressing its power over the sensible; idea of the infinite; mind comprehends beyond aesthetic understanding
findings.quote: The mathematical sublime challenges the imagination with objects of infinite scale, leading reason to intervene by expressing its power over the sensible

findings.antecedent: Natural phenomena (storms, earthquakes, dynamic sublime, Kant)
findings.consequent: Fear for one's safety; physical beings limited; mind judges nature without fear; vocation as being sublimely above nature
findings.quote: the dynamic sublime arises from encounters with natural phenomena like storms or earthquakes eliciting fear for one's safety.

findings.antecedent: Unpresentable dimension of art/landscape (disrupts established orders of language/continuous rhythm)
findings.consequent: Anxious pause; acute awareness of the 'here and now'; possibility of existence ceasing (Lyotard's sublime)
findings.quote: The sublime creates an anxious pause in this rhythm, holding it at bay.

findings.antecedent: Immediate experience in a landscape (entangled combination of sensations, emotions, memories, thoughts, and perceptions)
findings.source: Aesthetics and the Sublime: Why it Matters (p. 5)
findings.quote: 'Aesthetics as experience,' which suggests that our immediate experience in a landscape—as an entangled combination of sensations, emotions, memories, thoughts, and perceptions—is the source of aesthetic pleasure

findings.consequent: Shocks us out of habitual or commonsense relationships to ecology, materiality, and both human and more-than-human entities; reveals our interconnectedness to the world
findings.quote: Encountering the sublime in landscape presents the power to shock us out of habitual or commonsense relationships to ecology, materiality, and both human and more-than-human entities

findings.consequent: Affects the body as its primary vector; changes in the body's compositional state; physiological reaction before the mind is aware; produces 'unnatural tension and certain violent emotions of the nerves'
findings.quote: Burke (1757/2008) writes that the sublime is a force 'capable of affecting the body, and thus of exciting out passions'

findings.antecedent: Relations, movement, and physiological change (e.g., trembling, sweating)
findings.consequent: Emotion (bloc of bodily processes); then feelings (unconscious awareness of physical state); then conscious mental images (knowing a feeling)
findings.quote: Relations, movement and physiological change create emotion, not the reverse.

findings.consequent: Pre-conscious physiological changes; short-circuits pre-prepared emotions; hinders problem-solving; forces a moment of kinesthetic experimentation
findings.source: Once More - With Sensation This Time (p. 17)
findings.quote: The sublime breaks or at least temporarily short circuits these pre-prepared emotions, or it hinders the problem solving that the organism undertakes when faced with sensations

findings.antecedent: General 'conformation of their organs' in humans
findings.consequent: Sharedness in how sensation is understood and processed by the body before subjectivity; commonality in ideas post-sensation (Burke)
findings.source: Once More - With Sensation This Time (p. 18)
findings.quote: As all humans have a general 'conformation of their organs' there is a sharedness in how sensation is understood and processed by the body before subjectivity

findings.antecedent: Specific masses or compositions of rocks (mass, age, marks, geometric relationships, varying height/width/arrangement, removing vegetation, adjusting perceptual scales)
findings.consequent: Elicits experiences of the sublime; 'denote force'; aesthetic force; 'prehuman and nonrational' force (Whately's design principles)
findings.quote: Whately pays particular attention to how specific masses or compositions of rocks are strikingly capable of eliciting experiences of the sublime.

findings.antecedent: Dense fir plantation (saplings planted closely, uniform mass of black, extinction of form and color)
findings.consequent: Elicits some sense of the sublime; 'dreary image'; affectual relation through sensation, processed by 'theatre of the body' (Price's design principles)
findings.quote: Its appearance is indeed so uniformly dead and heavy, that instead of those cheering ideas which arise from the fresh luxuriant foliage...it has something of that dreary image, that extinction of form and colour

findings.antecedent: Subtly edited geologic material (monolithic masses, exposed rock) in Central Park
findings.consequent: Brings occupants into direct encounter with it; suggests its continuance beneath Manhattan; 'dramatized' the site's geologic forces (Olmsted's design)
findings.source: Olmsted Made Sublime Affects, He Didn't Just Conceptualize Them (p. 24)
findings.quote: this geologic material was subtly edited throughout the site to bring occupants into direct encounter with it, whilst also exposing it in monolithic masses that suggest its continuance beneath all of Manhattan

findings.antecedent: Labyrinthine path structure, constantly varying spatial perception, vegetation structures, and shifting landform (in The Ramble, Central Park)
findings.consequent: Disrupts sense of direction; produces a 'slow zone'; sense of introspection; individual appropriation of space; sense of time extends/lost; sense of space contracted; physiological response (minor or everyday sublime)
findings.source: Olmsted Made Sublime Affects, He Didn't Just Conceptualize Them (p. 25-26)
findings.quote: This slowing down involves a sense of introspection and an individual appropriation of space, where one's sense of time seems to extend and become lost, and sense of space is drastically contracted.

findings.antecedent: Physiological landscape-sublime (grounded in instigator material relations between the body and space-time)
findings.consequent: Becomes concrete, designable, and practical; allows for experimentation and modification in landscape production; works upwards from the material of landscape to illustrate what real experience actually is
findings.quote: This is the power of a physiological sublime for landscape architectural design: it works upwards from the material of landscape to illustrate what real experience actually is

findings.consequent: Disrupts pre-formed emotional responses ('habit-breaking affects'); 'lurking nearby, just around the corner waiting to explode into our experience' (the sublime)
findings.quote: Rather, the sublime can equally be found in the small and everyday as habit-breaking affects: physiological encounters that disrupt our pre-formed emotional responses.

limitations: The concept of the sublime tends to resist precise definition, leading to discourse collapsing into generalities (p. 2).
Lack of landscape architectural scholarship on the sublime (and aesthetics generally) due to characterization of non-machinic aspects as merely pictorial (p. 4).
Concern with how landscape 'really works' determined through disinterested objectivity, leading to a focus on computation over semiotics (p. 4).
Dismissal of the aesthetic dimension of landscape, rendering it superfluous by a naturalized, primarily functional conception (p. 4).
Environmental aesthetics scholarship (e.g., Carlson) often excludes the sublime due to its 'unacceptable degree of subjectivity' (p. 4).
Landscape experience is often regarded as 'merely subjective' compared to more objective design dimensions, leading to dismissal by academics and practitioners (p. 19).
minimum_safe_summary: This paper argues for a re-conceptualization of the sublime in landscape architecture, shifting its understanding from a psychological or subjective experience to a physiological event. Drawing on Edmund Burke's empirical work and Antonio Damasio's neuroaesthetics, the author proposes that the sublime emerges from pre-conscious bodily changes that disrupt habitual responses, fostering a sense of interconnectedness with the world. The paper illustrates this through historical design practices of Thomas Whately, Uvedale Price, and Frederick Law Olmsted, demonstrating how they manipulated elements like scale, material, and spatial configuration to elicit these physiological affects. Key findings include the idea that the sublime is a traceable and designable form of experience, operating before conscious thought and offering a means to create singular, habit-breaking encounters. Limitations acknowledged by the author include the historical difficulty in precisely defining the sublime and its dismissal in contemporary landscape architecture due to perceived subjectivity and a focus on technoscientific approaches.
